newsitem.title: GERMANY: German March M3 growth probably slowed-economists.
newsitem.headline: German March M3 growth probably slowed-economists.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth is likely to have stabilised in March, economists said on Friday, adding that recent comments from Bundesbank officials appeared to confirm their views.

In a Reuter poll, economists on average predicted that the annualised, seasonally-adjusted headline rate for M3 money supply growth would be 8.3 percent in March, with forecasts ranging from 8.1 to 8.6 percent.
This compares with February's 9.1 percent and January's 11.7 percent growth, both far above the central bank's 3.5 to 6.5 percent target growth corridor.
M3 money supply comprises cash in circulation, time, sight and savings deposits.
At the same time, economists said they expected the volume of funds in circulation to have increased.
"Overall we expect to see that money supply growth has calmed a bit," said Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of fixed income research at Trinkaus Capital Management in Duesseldorf.
The data are expected early next week, but the timing remains unclear as the Bundesbank declines to set a fixed release date beforehand.

Economists agreed that the driving force behind the expected slowdown would be a pick-up in long-term savings. Monetary capital formation, which had been weak for months but was showing signs of recovery in February, is likely to be have been a little bit stronger in March too.
But economists also said they did not expect to see a very strong pickup in monetary capital formation in future months, largely because investors still preferred to put their funds elsewhere.
"There would be a drastic increase in monetary capital formation only if two things occurred," said Irgeen Rust, a monetary economist at WestLB in Duesseldorf.

"Either capital market rates would have to surge much higher, to say around seven percent in one fell swoop, or investors would have to accept the fact that capital market rates are going to remain low for some time and overcome their aversion to investing at these levels, but it is unlikely that either thing is going to happen soon," she said.
Offsetting the slightly higher capital formation, however, is continuing strong lending to the private sector, economists said.
"Private sector lending is likely to have been quite strong, particularly as the economy is showing signs of picking up," said Eckhart Schulte, economist at IBJ in Frankfurt.
Looking ahead, economists see private sector lending picking up continually, especially as the economy regains steam in the summer months.
Consequently several economists said they did not expect the Bundesbank would hit its target corridor for M3 growth this year.
"We see a considerable increase in private sector lending and because of this, we also think it is unlikely that the corridor will be reached this year," IBJ's Schulte said.
On the other hand economists said comments by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing this week that March M3 likely stabilised sent a positive signal.
"Issing has already hinted at a stabilisation so this is very likely," WestLB's Rust said.
